In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spectroscopic factor quenching is not a simple function of the nuclear asymmetry.
the quenching of spectroscopic factors in neutron-rich nuclei is not a general phenomenon, but rather depends on the reaction mechanism.
the (p,d) spectroscopic factors of Ca40-48 and Ar34-46 isotopes are consistent with each other but inconsistent with the (p,d), one-nucleon-removal, and knockout results for Ca40-48 isotopes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
spectroscopic factors obtained from single-neutron transfer reactions are consistent with the dispersive optical-model analysis, while those obtained from knockout reactions are not.

the spectroscopic factors of Ca40-46 isotopes are consistent between (p,d) and (e,e') measurements, while the (p,d) spectroscopic factors of neutron-rich Ca isotopes are consistent with the dispersive optical-model analysis.
spectroscopic factors extracted from single-neutron knockout reactions are systematically lower than those from transfer reactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
spectroscopic factors are not necessarily reliable probes of nuclear correlations.

the (p,d) reaction can be used as a reliable probe to extract spectroscopic factors in the neutron-rich region, and the spectroscopic factors obtained from the (p,d)-reaction are in good agreement with those from dispersive optical-model analysis.
spectroscopic factors are sensitive to both the initial and final nuclear wave functions.
